Enquiry 1: Rainforest Kingdom — Ogiso Rulers, Red-Earth Walls and Anglo-Saxon Contrast (c. AD 900–1180)

Big Question: How did Edo communities build a vast rainforest kingdom by AD 900?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Edo (E-do) Ogiso (O-gi-so) Iya (I-ya) Laterite (Lat-er-ite) Palm Oil (Palm Oil)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Sculpted Terracotta Head From Benin City’s Brass-Casters’ Quarter (16th–17th Century Tradition, Rooted in Early Edo Clay Art)
Rainforest Craft Clue: Long before European ships arrived, Edo sculptors modelled lifelike terracotta and metal heads for sacred altars!

1a. Look at Source B. How can you tell these iron eben swords were made for royal ceremonies rather than battlefield fighting?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source B, historians can tell these iron eben swords were ceremonial symbols of royal power because..."
Word Bank: leaf-shaped • iron blacksmiths • Ogiso • royal authority
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Linked red-clay Iya ditches and banks stretch across 500+ Edo rainforest settlements (c. AD 1100)
Early Edo farming villages clear sunlit rainforest plots for yams and oil palms (c. AD 500–800)
Anglo-Saxon rulers in Britain build smaller timber burh forts while Ogiso rule Edo (c. AD 900)
Edo elders banish the last Ogiso ruler and invite help from sacred Ife (c. AD 1180)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Oba Ewedo moves the royal palace to its grand central site in Benin City (c. AD 1255)
Oba Ozolua expands Benin’s power before Oba Esigie’s sixteenth-century Golden Age (c. AD 1480)

Increased brass manilla trade lets Igun Street casters pour hundreds of detailed court plaques (c. AD 1500)

Enquiry 4: Sacred Court Rituals — The Oba, Queen Mother Idia and Everyday Edo Life (c. AD 1500–1700)

TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue

Enquiry 5: Global Traders — Brass Manillas, Cowrie Shells and European Visitors (c. AD 1485–1850)

Big Question: Why were European visitors so amazed by Benin’s trade and wide streets?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Gwato Port (Gwa-to Port) Ambassador (Am-bas-sa-dor) Manillas (Ma-nil-las) Cowrie Shells (Cow-rie Shells) Olfert Dapper (Ol-fert Dap-per)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Benin Brass Plaque of Two Portuguese Merchants Holding Manillas (16th–17th Century)
Trade Metal Clue: Benin exported pepper, cloth, and ivory in exchange for European brass manillas—then melted manillas into African art!

1a. Inspect Source A. What trade goods are the two bearded Portuguese visitors holding, and how did these boost Benin’s art?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the two bearded Portuguese merchants are holding stacks of..."
Word Bank: brass manillas • Benin pepper • Igun Street • lost-wax casting
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Dutch scholar Olfert Dapper publishes merchant accounts praising Benin’s 30 wide clean streets (AD 1668)
Portuguese explorer João Afonso de Aveiro reaches Gwato port and visits Benin City (AD 1485)
English Captain Thomas Windham meets a Benin Oba speaking fluent Portuguese (AD 1553)
The Oba sends a royal Benin ambassador by ship to King Manuel’s court in Lisbon (c. AD 1514)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 6: 1897 British Invasion, Looted Bronzes and Living Edo Heritage Today (1897–Present)

Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A taken inside the Oba’s palace on 18 February 1897, this photograph proves..."

Oba Ovonramwen Nogbaisi becomes Oba and defends Benin’s palm-oil trade tolls (AD 1888)
The Benin monarchy is restored under Oba Eweka II while Igun Street revives royal casting (AD 1914)
Twelve hundred British troops capture Benin City, exile Ovonramwen, and loot 4,000+ bronzes (Feb 1897)
